Lake Ira Lalaro is the largest lake in Timor-Leste. It is a seasonal body of water, whose size expands greatly during the wet season, from 1,000 hectares to 5,500 hectares. The northern shore is flat grassland that reclaims much of the lake during the dry season, while the southern shore is swampy with half drowned trees, more photogenic but harder to reach. It is hard is really appreciate the lake without using a drone as the landscape is so flat. The lake is apparently home to around 300 crocodiles, so be careful! Note that the road around the southern shore of the lake to Jaco Island is only passable by motorbike, and then only if you are comfortable driving over a rudimentary wooden bridge.

The best known hot springs in the country were developed by the Portuguese, with a resort complex built around the pools, but fell into disrepair. In 2016 the whole complex was redeveloped, but little maintenance appears to have taken place since. As of 2024 the toilets are completely out of action, and derelict buildings surround the pools. The hot springs produce ~2,000 litres of water per minute. There are three pools, one very hot (up to ~50C), one hot, and one cold. Despite only being 55km from Dili, allow at least 5 hours to get there, along increasingly bad roads that require good off-road skills.

I have visited Atauro Island twice, first in 2025 and again in 2026, and every visit has reminded me why this island is considered one of the hidden jewels of the Coral Triangle.
Atauro is home to some of the richest marine biodiversity in the world, with crystal-clear waters, vibrant coral reefs, and incredible opportunities for snorkeling and diving. Beyond its natural beauty, the island’s communities are deeply connected to marine conservation.

Jaco Island, located off the eastern coast of Timor-Leste, is a pristine tropical haven that enchants visitors with its untouched beauty. Accessible only by boat, the island is a sanctuary of powdery white sands surrounded by turquoise waters, creating a postcard-perfect setting. Snorkelers and divers revel in the vibrant coral reefs, encountering an array of marine life beneath the crystalline surface. With no permanent inhabitants and limited infrastructure, Jaco offers a serene escape for those seeking tranquility. Its unspoiled landscapes, coupled with the warm hospitality of locals, make Jaco Island a true paradise for nature enthusiasts and adventurers alike.

reviews.textTranslated: An uninhabited island at the easternmost tip of the island. After reaching Tutuala, which isn't easy due to the poor state of the roads, the descent to the channel separating East Timor from Jaco Island—now paved, once a dirt track—is an 8km journey with the expectation of successfully crossing the channel, though this isn't always reliable due to sea conditions. The crossing is provided by willing fishermen for $10 per person. Lunch can be negotiated with the fisherman, as you can always find fish for your meal during the crossing. Overnight stays on the island are prohibited. Snorkeling is allowed, and sunscreen is recommended. The warm, blue waters, picture-perfect, offer no rest, as being in the water is more than obligatory. This is one of the experiences not to be missed by anyone visiting East Timor; a little tiring, admittedly, but worthwhile. Don't miss it.

reviews.text: Jaco Island, located off the eastern coast of Timor-Leste, is a pristine tropical haven that enchants visitors with its untouched beauty. Accessible only by boat, the island is a sanctuary of powdery white sands surrounded by turquoise waters, creating a postcard-perfect setting. Snorkelers and divers revel in the vibrant coral reefs, encountering an array of marine life beneath the crystalline surface. With no permanent inhabitants and limited infrastructure, Jaco offers a serene escape for those seeking tranquility. Its unspoiled landscapes, coupled with the warm hospitality of locals, make Jaco Island a true paradise for nature enthusiasts and adventurers alike.

Anfahrt mit Roller möglich, aber schon eine Herausforderung. Gerade nach Regen ist die Piste sehr schlammig. Teils so tiefe Pfützen, dass man nur Barfuß durchkommt oder eben mit dem Roller. Am Parkplatz campierten an einem Sonntag geschätzt 2.000 Menschen, meist Teenies. Ich bin um 9 Uhr losgelaufen und war um 10:20 Uhr am Gipfel. Weg sehr einfach zu gehen, teils mit Treppen. Auf dem Weg etliche Stände mit Getränken und Suppen. Beim Wandern leben die Teenies ihre Jugendkultur voll aus, hören laute Musik, schreien herum, werfen ihren Müll in die Natur. Ich hab mehrere Tüten davon aufgesammelt, aber da liegt leider noch genug herum. Gottes Schöpfung wird hier völlig missachtet. Ganz anderes Bild am Gipfel. An der Marienstatue wird gebeten und dem Herren gelobt. Alle sind leise und ehrfürchtig. Es ist ein Wallfahrtsort.
Es war schön zu sehen, dass so viele junge Leute Bergsteigen gehen. Die meisten sehr freundlich. Als einziger Europäischer bin ich auf viel Begeisterung gestoßen. Ist sicherlich nicht jedermanns Sache, aber ich vermute, dass es unter der Woche ruhiger ist.

For an independent traveler get a minitruck (3$)from Taibesi station in Dili. Look for the name „Hatu Builico“ on the trucks. From my understanding there’s a truck at a specific date and time that goes directly to Hatu Builico, the village near the summit. If it doesn’t (that happened to me) tell the driver you‘ll go to Mt. Ramelau. He‘ll drop you at the place called „Fleixa“ about 8 km after Maubisse. There‘s a sign „Mt. Ramelau“ pointing to a very bad unpaved road on the right. If you walk on this road, it‘s 18 km to Hatu Builico. The road is very scenic. In my case I met a villager from Hatu Builico and I just walked with him. He used cow paths and walked in straight line from Fleixa to Hatu Builico. This reduces the distance and took me only 2 hours to reach Hatu Builico but I wouldn’t attempt this if I was alone.
In Hatu Builico the villagers are very nice and friendly. Some can speak English and can help you find a hotel. From the village it‘s straightforward 4 km to the trail entrance and another 4 km to the summit.
If 18 km walking back to Fleixa doesn’t appeal to you, your hotel can arrange a transport either motorbike or 4WD for you. I paid 30$ for a ride with a motorbike to Maubisse.

Getting there by scooter is possible, but quite a challenge. Especially after rain, the track is very muddy. In some places, the puddles are so deep that you can only get through barefoot or by scooter. On a Sunday, an estimated 2,000 people, mostly teenagers, were camping in the parking lot. I started hiking at 9:00 a.m. and reached the summit at 10:20 a.m. The trail is very easy to walk, partly with steps. There are several stalls selling drinks and soup along the way. While hiking, the teenagers fully embrace their youth culture, listening to loud music, shouting, and throwing their trash into nature. I picked up several bags of it, but unfortunately, there's still plenty lying around. God's creation is completely disregarded here. A completely different scene unfolds at the summit. At the statue of Mary, people pray and praise the Lord. Everyone is quiet and reverent. It's a place of pilgrimage.

It was wonderful to see so many young people going mountaineering. Most of them were very friendly. As the only European, I encountered a great deal of enthusiasm. It's certainly not for everyone, but I suspect it's quieter during the week.

Overall worthwhile, but the amount of trash and noise is very sad. Please consider how Jesus or Mary would have reacted here. I'm sure they wouldn't have approved of all this garbage and waste on the mountain.

And please wear sturdy shoes for the mountain. No flip-flops or sandals.

reviews.name: Arthit Yodyunyong
reviews.text:
For an independent traveler get a minitruck (3$)from Taibesi station in Dili. Look for the name „Hatu Builico“ on the trucks. From my understanding there’s a truck at a specific date and time that goes directly to Hatu Builico, the village near the summit. If it doesn’t (that happened to me) tell the driver you‘ll go to Mt. Ramelau. He‘ll drop you at the place called „Fleixa“ about 8 km after Maubisse. There‘s a sign „Mt. Ramelau“ pointing to a very bad unpaved road on the right. If you walk on this road, it‘s 18 km to Hatu Builico. The road is very scenic. In my case I met a villager from Hatu Builico and I just walked with him. He used cow paths and walked in straight line from Fleixa to Hatu Builico. This reduces the distance and took me only 2 hours to reach Hatu Builico but I wouldn’t attempt this if I was alone.
In Hatu Builico the villagers are very nice and friendly. Some can speak English and can help you find a hotel. From the village it‘s straightforward 4 km to the trail entrance and another 4 km to the summit.
If 18 km walking back to Fleixa doesn’t appeal to you, your hotel can arrange a transport either motorbike or 4WD for you. I paid 30$ for a ride with a motorbike to Maubisse.

reviews.textTranslated:
If you're planning to see the Christ the Redeemer statue, you absolutely must read this.

To get to the statue, you can rent a scooter or drive yourself.

If you want to take a city bus, you can catch the blue bus number 12 near Largo de Lecidere Park. The fare is $0.25.

For two people, it's $0.50.

The bus platform is small, so seats aren't guaranteed. You'll have to squeeze in.

We went at 11 am, and we really regretted it...

The reason is that the UV radiation in East Timor is terrifying!

My goodness! Although the temperature was only 27 degrees Celsius, the UV index here was over 10, which is dangerous.

I recommend coming very early in the morning, or after 4 pm. Definitely don't come around noon. I got dizzy and had a headache after walking for an hour. Everyone visiting East Timor must wear sunscreen and a hat.

You can park on the outskirts. If you ride in, there's a parking lot, but it costs $1.

There are two ways to get up; just take the outer path.

We parked the car and then walked halfway around the bay, going up from the back beach.

The Christ the Redeemer statue doesn't look very tall, but climbing it is still quite tiring... The main reason is the heat! 🥵🥵🥵

Make sure to bring electrolytes or buy some coconuts to drink; the sun here is even more intense than in Bali, Indonesia! 🫠
